name: Uma Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm 27 and I work in marketing at Shinewell, a brand that makes cleaning sprays and washing liquid, at their offices next to the factory. I write the words on the bottles, the back labels and the little promise on the front, and I plan the leaflets and shelf deals for the supermarkets. It's not glamorous, but there's a rhythm to it I like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know every product by heart; I could tell you the scent names of all twelve sprays. What wears me out is that the team got smaller last spring when Ken left and wasn't replaced, so I've picked up his leaflets too. I'm on the lower side for pay, and Deniz, my boyfriend, drives a bus, so we're careful, and we've got under a month saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've seen what they write and it all sounds the same, like a hotel brochure. My manager, Carol, hasn't pushed it, and I'm happy to keep doing it my way as long as nobody makes me change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So mostly nothing happens. That sounds like Shinewell already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and leave it there. I don't really post about things like this. At work I'd just say, back to the labels then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be worried, just not about AI. They didn't replace Ken, and nobody told us why. If they did that once to save money, they can do it again, and I'm the one with the lowest pay to cut or the easiest job to share out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work well, especially the leaflets, so nobody can say Ken's work dropped. I'd put twenty a week aside, even if it means fewer takeaways. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs board, though there's hardly anything round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit stuck. It's not the robots, it's the quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by the quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody says anything at Shinewell. My colleague Ken's desk was just empty one Monday, and I keep thinking it'll be my desk one Monday. Carol said he'd moved on, and nobody will say anything when it's mine either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it was your desk, what would you do that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring my mum, first. Then I'd go to the supermarket where I used to work on Saturdays as a student and ask for shifts. It's not marketing, but it's money while I look.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised** and leave it there.
At work I'd just say it's **back to the labels** and carry on.
think: I think the risk is **cost-cutting**, not AI.
They didn't **replace Ken**, so my desk could be next.
do: Do the **leaflets** well so nobody says Ken's work dropped.
Put **twenty a week** aside, even with fewer takeaways.
Keep an eye on the **local jobs board**.
feel: I feel **uneasy and stuck**, worried more by the quiet than robots.
S0.quote: My colleague Ken's desk was just empty one Monday, and I keep thinking it'll be my desk one Monday.
fieldNote: Her fear comes from a **colleague's quiet exit**, not from AI.
She would **dig in** and work harder rather than look around much.
Her fallback is **supermarket shifts**, which she did as a student.

steps.text: Take on Ken's leaflets and keep them to standard
Put twenty a week aside by cutting takeaways
Watch the local jobs board without applying yet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking first. That's the labels. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it's business, firms will use whatever's cheaper, and people need to keep up. I'd probably not say much more than that. I'm not someone who goes to marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm the one who goes. If a computer can write back labels and plan leaflets, Shinewell keeps one person to check the words and that person isn't me, because I've never touched the tools. Carol would keep whoever's quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Carol directly whether there's a place for me somewhere else at Shinewell, maybe checking the product claims with the quality team. I'd cut back hard: no holiday this year, cheaper phone plan. I'd hold off learning the AI as long as I could, honestly, but if Carol said it was that or the door, I'd sit with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. Like waiting for the post on results day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off learning the AI. Why wait, if it might save your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not good with new things, and I don't want to look slow in front of everyone. It's stupid, I know. I'd rather be good at the old way than bad at the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Deniz say, if you came home and told him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we'll manage on his wage for a bit, and we would, just about. But he does long shifts and I'd hate being the one who made them longer.

say: I'd say it's **business**, and firms use whatever's cheaper.
I'd say people need to **keep up**, but I wouldn't **march**.
think: I think I'm **the one who goes**, since I've never used the tools.
Shinewell would keep **one checker**, and my manager Carol keeps the **quicker one**.
do: Ask Carol about a role with the **quality team** checking product claims.
Cut back hard: **no holiday** and a cheaper phone plan.
Learn the **AI tools** only if Carol says it's that or leave.
feel: I feel **sick in my stomach**, like waiting for exam results.
S1.quote: I'd rather be good at the old way than bad at the new one.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and knows her resistance makes it likelier.
Her **pride** keeps her from learning the tools early.
Her partner's **bus wage** is a thin backstop she feels guilty using.

steps.text: Ask Carol about moving to the quality team at Shinewell
Skip this year's holiday and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Hold off learning the AI unless Carol makes it a condition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's nothing. That's two Christmases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and that the government should have planned for it. I'd say it to my family, mainly, not online. People would be scared, and I wouldn't want to add to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of marketing by 2028, no question. A cleaning brand isn't going to pay me to write about lemon spray when the AI can do it in a second. The robots come around 2031, so Deniz's bus job is safe for a few years, and that's what we'd live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to the supermarket and ask for shifts straight away, even before I lost the job, just to have a foot in. We'd stop saving for a deposit and use that money to pay bills. I'd ask my parents if they could help with rent for a few months. We'd put off getting engaged; we'd talked about next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. But at least one of us has a job you need hands for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the supermarket work itself? Robots come there too, eventually.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. Around 2031, by your card. Three years of shelf stacking and tills is not a plan; it's a waiting room. It's three years to think, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off the engagement. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deniz would say it doesn't matter, a ring's a ring. But my mum would be upset, and so would I, a bit. It's the thing we were looking forward to.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and government should have planned.
I'd talk to **family**, not online, so I don't add to the fear.
think: I think I'm **out of marketing** by 2028, no question.
Deniz's **bus job** lasts until robots come, around 2031.
do: Ask the supermarket for **shifts** straight away, before losing the job.
Use the **deposit savings** for bills and ask my parents for help.
Put off our **engagement** planned for next summer.
feel: I feel **scared**, but glad one of us has a **hands-on job**.
S2.quote: Three years of shelf stacking and tills is not a plan; it's a waiting room.
fieldNote: She sees **supermarket work** as a stopgap, not a future.
Her partner's **hands-on job** becomes the household's anchor.
AGI would delay their **engagement**, which hurts more than she lets on.

steps.text: Ask the supermarket where she worked as a student for shifts
Ask her parents to help with rent for a few months
Put off the engagement planned for next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I'd be 32. That's still young enough to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so firms and the government should put on proper courses. I'd keep it practical, no big opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still lose the job around 2031. But five years means I could train for something before it goes. I'd want something with my hands and with people, since the robots don't come until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Shinewell as long as they'll have me and save hard, maybe thirty a week. I'd look at a dental nurse course. My cousin Elif did a dental nurse course and she's never short of work. I'd start it in the second year, part-time, when I'd seen it was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried. It keeps me awake some nights, but I'd have something to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a dental nurse, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elif says it's steady, it's hands-on, and people always need their teeth done. She showed me the course. It's a year part-time, which I could do in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year before starting. What would you be waiting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To see if it's actually happening, I suppose. That's me, I don't jump. But I'd know that waiting too long would be the worst thing I could do.

say: I'd say firms and government should put on **proper courses**.
I'd keep it **practical** and say what helps, without big opinions about who is to blame.
think: I think I'd still **lose the job** around 2031.
Five years lets me train for **hands-on work** before robots arrive.
do: Stay at Shinewell and **save thirty a week**.
Start a part-time **dental nurse course** in the second year.
Ask my cousin Elif how she **found work** after her course.
feel: I feel **still worried**, but now I have something to do.
S3.quote: My cousin Elif did a dental nurse course and she's never short of work.
fieldNote: She'd still **lose her job**, but time lets her choose a trade.
Her **cautious streak** shows: she'd wait a year before starting.
She draws on **family examples** rather than news or experts.

steps.text: Save thirty a week while staying at Shinewell
Start a part-time dental nurse course in year two
Wait a year to see if AGI is really coming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time to sort it out properly, and the government should. I wouldn't make a fuss; I'd expect them to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd ride it out at Shinewell for a good few years, maybe learn some of the tools late, and then switch. It's still the end of my job, but it's far enough away that I'd probably put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Shinewell, save what I can, and get engaged next summer like we planned. Around year four or five, I'd start the dental nurse course. I'd learn the AI tools only when Carol made us all do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Uneasy, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably put it off. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I know myself. With ten years, I'll say next year, next year, and my boyfriend Deniz would have to give me a push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change your plans with Deniz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we'd go ahead with the engagement and maybe even the flat. We'd still be careful with money. But we wouldn't be living like it's an emergency.

say: I'd say the government has **plenty of time** to sort it properly.
I wouldn't **make a fuss**; I'd expect them to act.
think: I think I'd **ride it out** at Shinewell for years.
It's still **the end** of my job, but I'd put it off.
do: Keep going at Shinewell and **save what I can**.
Go ahead with **the engagement** next summer.
Start the **dental nurse course** around year four or five.
feel: I feel **calmer**: uneasy, but I **can breathe**.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'll say next year, next year, and my boyfriend Deniz would have to give me a push.
fieldNote: The long warning lets her **keep life plans** like the engagement.
She knows she'll **delay** and relies on her partner to push.
She'd still **lose her job** by 2036, which keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Keep writing labels at Shinewell and save what she can
Put money aside for the engagement and a flat deposit
Start a dental nurse course around year four or five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to learn anything, and we'd be living on one wage. What would help is being told early, honestly, and a course paid for by someone who isn't me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about people who aren't keen on change. Everyone says adapt, adapt. Some of us need a hand to get going, not a lecture.

headlineQuote: Everyone says adapt, adapt. Some of us need a hand to get going, not a lecture.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old label writer** at a cleaning products brand, on low pay with little saved.
She has **never used AI** and prefers to stay good at the old way.
She's pragmatic, sees AI as **just business**, and avoids public fuss.
She's **anxious** even in the calm picture, after a colleague left and wasn't replaced.
With time she'd train as a **dental nurse**, though she knows she'll delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to learn and the couple on one wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid-for course**, not one she has to fund herself.
